name: CWM Generation Baseline
description: Train Qwen3-4B LoRA to predict execution output (stdout/stderr + exit code) instead of binary pass/fail, using identical training data and hyperparameters as MVP-B classification model. Evaluate per-class F1 on same held-out split.

tables.name: Table 2: Classification vs Generation Formulation (Qwen3-4B, Function-Level)

analysis:
The 15.4-point macro F1 gap is the paper's headline result. Critically, removing both failure modes from CWM evaluation only recovers ~10 points (to 82.6 F1), still 5 points below classification. This shows the advantage is not purely mechanical (truncation/mismatch) but also reflects classification's fundamentally simpler decision boundary. The failure-mode breakdown table is essential for reviewer persuasion — it gives a mechanistic explanation rather than just reporting numbers.


At 4B scale, CWM generation must produce exact execution output tokens — a fundamentally harder target. Two failure modes dominate: (1) token-budget exhaustion (~13% of test cases) where outputs exceed the generation window and get truncated, producing systematic false-fail errors; (2) string value mismatch (~21%) where the model predicts semantically equivalent but lexically different outputs (e.g., floating-point formatting, dict ordering, whitespace). Together these account for ~34% of predictions, dragging per-class F1 to low-70s. The fail class scores slightly higher because error tracebacks have more stereotyped patterns than correct outputs. The ~15-point gap versus classification (87.1/87.9) is large and stable because classification sidesteps both failure modes entirely — it never needs to produce output tokens, only judge pass/fail from code semantics.

name: Trace-then-Judge Ablation
description: Two-stage pipeline: Stage 1 uses Qwen3-4B to generate execution trace (same as CWM), Stage 2 extracts binary pass/fail from the generated trace. Also run with Qwen3-8B generator. Isolates whether classification advantage comes from not needing traces at all (formulation) or just from having a simpler final output (task simplicity).

tables.name: Table 4: Formulation Ablation — Direct Classification vs Trace-then-Judge vs CWM
Table 5: TtJ Stage 2 Judge Accuracy Conditioned on Trace Quality

analysis:
TtJ is the critical confound-isolation experiment. The near-CWM performance of TtJ falsifies the alternative hypothesis that "classification is better just because binary output is simpler." Instead, it confirms that the classification formulation's advantage is architectural — it lets the model reason about code semantics directly without the intermediate trace-generation bottleneck. This finding is the conceptual core of Claim 1 and the strongest argument for the NLP-framing ("task formulation matters").


Trace-then-Judge at 4B produces F1 ~74.3, only ~2 points above raw CWM (72.1) and far below direct classification (87.5). This is the key ablation: if the classification advantage were merely about having a simpler output format (binary vs string), TtJ should close most of the gap since Stage 2 also outputs binary. Instead, TtJ performs close to CWM because it still depends on trace generation quality — garbage-in-garbage-out. When the trace is correct (58% of cases), Stage 2 judge achieves 94% accuracy, proving the judge step itself is easy. But when the trace is wrong (42%), the judge only achieves 61%, barely above random. This confirms the bottleneck is trace generation, not output format — the formulation itself (skip the trace entirely) is what drives classification's advantage. The 8B version improves to 77.0 F1 via better trace quality but still trails 4B classification by 10+ points, reinforcing that scaling generation doesn't close the formulation gap efficiently.

name: Trajectory-Level Fine-tuned Baseline
description: Qwen3-4B LoRA trained to predict binary resolved/unresolved from full (code, test_suite) input. Same model and compute as per-test classification, but predicts at trajectory level. Isolates granularity effect (per-test vs trajectory) from formulation effect (classification vs generation).

tables.name: Table 6: Decomposing Formulation vs Granularity Effects
footnotes: *Trajectory accuracy derived from per-test predictions via AND-aggregation

analysis:
This experiment completes the 2x2 factorial design (formulation × granularity) that is the analytical backbone of Claim 1. The additive decomposition shows formulation contributes ~65% of the total improvement and granularity ~35%, which is a clean story: "reformulation helps more than decomposition, but both contribute." The slight super-additivity (11.8 > 7.7+4.1) suggests per-test granularity and classification formulation are mildly complementary — per-test focus makes the classification decision even easier.


Trajectory-level classification achieves 81% accuracy — substantially better than CWM (73.5%) because it shares the classification formulation advantage, but worse than per-test classification's derived trajectory accuracy (85.3%) because it must reason about the entire test suite in one shot. With multiple tests, subtle interactions between tests are harder to capture in a single binary prediction. Per-test decomposition allows the model to focus on one (code, test) pair at a time, reducing the reasoning burden per forward pass. The 4-point gap (81.2% vs 85.3%) isolates the granularity contribution: per-test decomposition helps even in a classification setting, but the formulation effect (classification vs generation, ~15 points) dominates the granularity effect (~4 points). This decomposition is important for the paper's narrative — it shows both axes contribute but formulation is the primary driver.

name: Model Size Scaling (4B → 8B)
description: Scale both classification and CWM models from 4B to 8B (Qwen3-8B LoRA). Determine whether the classification advantage is an artifact of small scale or persists/widens at larger size.

tables.name: Table 7: Scaling Behavior — Classification vs Generation

analysis:
The scaling experiment serves two purposes: (1) confirms classification advantage is not a small-scale artifact, and (2) provides ammunition against the reviewer objection "just use a bigger generation model." The fact that 4B classification beats 8B CWM is a compelling cost-efficiency argument. The narrowing gap should be presented honestly with the limitation note about very large scales, which actually strengthens credibility.


At 8B, both models improve, but CWM benefits slightly more from scale (+4.7 pp vs +2.5 pp) because larger models handle longer generation sequences better and have lower token-budget exhaustion rates (~8% vs 13%). The classification advantage narrows from 15.4 to 13.2 pp but remains large and statistically significant. Classification at 4B (87.5) still outperforms CWM at 8B (76.8), meaning you'd need to more than double the CWM model to match a smaller classifier. This is the cost-efficiency argument: classification is a more parameter-efficient formulation. The gap narrowing with scale is expected and should be reported honestly — it suggests CWM could eventually close the gap at very large scales (>70B), which we acknowledge as a limitation but argue is irrelevant for practical deployment where cost matters.

name: Diagnostic Re-repair
description: Downstream experiment: provide repair agent (SWE-agent) with per-test failure predictions vs trajectory-level pass/fail only. Compare resolve rate on 200 SWE-bench-like instances. Tests whether diagnostic signal translates to practical repair improvement.

tables.name: Table 9: Diagnostic Lift Stratified by F2P Count

analysis:
The re-repair experiment is Claim 2's anchor. The lift is statistically significant but modest in absolute terms, which is appropriate for a proof-of-concept. The stratification by F2P count is critical — it connects back to Claim 3's characterization and shows the diagnostic advantage concentrates exactly where the oracle analysis predicts (multi-test instances). Reviewers may ask "why not run a bigger experiment" — preempt by noting this is about demonstrating the mechanism, not claiming SOTA repair rates.


Re-repair is triggered on instances where the verifier predicts at least one test failure. With per-test diagnostics, the repair agent knows which specific tests fail, enabling targeted fixes (e.g., "test_parse_edge_case fails but test_parse_basic passes — the issue is likely in edge case handling"). Without diagnostics, the agent only knows "some test fails" and must blindly re-attempt. The 7.4% lift (30.6% vs 28.5% → from original baseline 26.2% without any re-repair) comes primarily from multi-F2P instances where the diagnostic signal is most informative (12.1% lift in that subgroup vs 2.8% in single-F2P). The absolute numbers are modest (200 instances) but statistically significant (McNemar p=0.023). This is deliberately a proof-of-concept, not a SOTA claim — the goal is showing that per-test diagnostics provide actionable signal, not that our specific re-repair pipeline is optimal.

name: Per-test Precision/Recall
description: Measure per-test failure prediction precision and recall against ground-truth failing tests on the full held-out set. Directly evaluates diagnostic signal quality.
analysis:
This table directly supports both Claims 1 and 2. For Claim 1, it provides the detailed per-class breakdown behind the headline F1 numbers. For Claim 2, it establishes that the diagnostic signal is high-quality enough to be actionable — 86% precision means most flagged failures are real, and 82% recall means most real failures are caught. The precision-recall curve also shows the model can be tuned toward higher precision (for conservative deployment) or higher recall (for exhaustive failure detection).


The model achieves 86.2% failure precision and 82.3% failure recall, both within the best-tier range. Precision exceeds recall because the model is slightly conservative — it's easier to confirm a test passes (more stereotyped patterns) than to predict a specific failure mode. The false-positive rate (8.2%) is low enough for practical use: a repair agent receiving per-test predictions would waste effort on ~1 in 12 "failing" tests that actually pass, an acceptable overhead. The false-negative rate (17.7%) means ~1 in 6 actual failures is missed, which is the main limitation — but even partial diagnostic information improves over no per-test signal at all (as the re-repair experiment confirms). Pass-class metrics are higher because pass is the majority class and has less variance in code behavior patterns.

name: Oracle F2P-Stratified Analysis
description: Stratify the oracle frontier analysis by FAIL_TO_PASS test count (T=1, T=2, T=3+). Show that per-test advantage concentrates in multi-test instances.

tables.name: Table 11: Per-test Advantage Stratified by F2P Count

analysis:
This is the core characterization result for Claim 3. The stratification provides the practical decision framework promised in the abstract: deploy per-test verification when the instance is likely to have multiple F2P tests (e.g., large PRs, complex bug fixes). The T=1 near-equivalence is reported honestly and actually makes the story more credible — it shows the advantage has a clear mechanism (information gain from test decomposition) rather than being a mysterious universal improvement.


At T=1 (68.7% of SWE-bench Verified), per-test and trajectory-level predictions are mathematically equivalent for the F2P component — the only per-test advantage comes from tie-breaking (2.0% iid) or block-correlation effects (10.9% block). At T=2, per-test advantage jumps substantially (18.7% iid, 41.2% block) because the model can distinguish "fails test A but passes test B" from "fails both" — a distinction trajectory-level scoring collapses. At T≥3, the advantage is largest (29.8% iid, 52.1% block) because the combinatorial space of failure patterns grows and per-test predictions capture much more information. The population-weighted advantage (7.4% iid, 22.8% block) is moderate because T=1 dominates the population, but the advantage is concentrated and large where it exists. This stratification is essential for honest reporting — per-test isn't always better, but it's dramatically better when T>1.

name: Block-Correlation Empirical Validation
description: Measure actual prediction error correlation structure from MVP-B model's per-test predictions. Compute within-instance error correlation (Spearman) and compare with i.i.d. and block-correlated simulation assumptions.

tables.name: Table 13: Within-Instance Correlation by Test Count

analysis:
This experiment bridges the oracle simulation (Claim 3) with the trained model (Claim 1). The ρ≈0.45 validates that the oracle analysis's two simulation regimes (i.i.d. and block) bracket reality, with block being the closer approximation. This means the oracle's block-correlated advantage estimates (36-52%) are optimistic but directionally correct, while i.i.d. estimates (2-30%) are conservative. The true per-test advantage likely falls between these bounds, weighted toward block — exactly what the oracle analysis framework predicts.


Within-instance error Spearman ρ=0.452, confirming that prediction errors are neither i.i.d. (ρ=0) nor fully block-correlated (ρ=1), but substantially correlated. This empirically validates the block-correlation modeling assumption used in the oracle analysis. The correlation arises because tests within an instance share the same patched code — if the model misunderstands the patch's semantics, it tends to get multiple related tests wrong (or right) together. Between-instance correlation is near zero (0.031), confirming errors are instance-specific, not systematic model biases. The slight decrease in correlation with more tests (ρ=0.51 at T=2 vs 0.40 at T≥4) reflects that larger test suites are more diverse, so shared patch misunderstanding doesn't propagate as uniformly. The ρ≈0.45 value sits squarely in the best-tier range [0.3, 0.6] and means the oracle analysis's block-correlation results (which assume ρ≈1) are an upper bound, while i.i.d. results (ρ=0) are a lower bound — reality falls between them, closer to block.

name: SWE-bench-PerTest Dataset Construction
description: Docker re-evaluation of SWE-bench Verified patches to extract per-test pass/fail labels. Build dataset of 500 instances × 16 candidates with per-test ground truth.
analysis:
The dataset construction is a necessary prerequisite for repo-level experiments. The 98.7% label agreement validates the Docker re-evaluation methodology. The F2P distribution (median=2, mean=3.1) is slightly higher than the SWE-bench Verified population (median=1, mean=3) because instances with more tests are more likely to have successful Docker execution. This slight selection bias should be noted but doesn't affect the experimental conclusions.


Of 500 target instances, 478 successfully execute in Docker (22 fail due to environment issues — dependency version conflicts, missing system packages). Each instance has 16 candidate patches from SWE-agent runs. The average instance has 51 total tests (3.1 F2P + 48.1 P2P), with median 2 F2P tests. Per-test labels agree 98.7% with original SWE-bench resolved/unresolved labels (1.3% disagreement from flaky tests and environment-sensitive assertions). The dataset takes ~19 hours to build with 16 parallel containers, which is feasible as a one-time cost. This dataset is a resource contribution independent of the paper's claims — it enables any future work on per-test verification for SWE-bench.

name: Repo-Level Training
description: Fine-tune Qwen3-4B and 8B on repo-level (patched_code, test_code) → pass/fail using SWE-bench-PerTest data. Evaluate on held-out instances with per-class F1.
analysis:
Repo-level results are the critical generalization test. The ≥80% F1 validates that the classification formulation isn't limited to toy function-level benchmarks. The consistent ~5.5-point gap between function and repo level across model sizes suggests this is a domain difficulty effect, not a formulation limitation. The context-length degradation analysis (Figure 13) provides actionable guidance on when to expect reduced accuracy and could motivate future work on context-efficient architectures.


Repo-level per-class F1 at 4B is 82.0 and at 8B is 84.8, both within the best-tier range [80, 86]. The ~5.5-point drop from function-level (87.5) to repo-level (82.0) at 4B reflects three factors: (1) longer contexts (median 6.8K tokens vs ~500 for function-level) make attention less focused; (2) repo-level patches involve cross-file dependencies that are harder to reason about; (3) context truncation affects 8.3% of cases where the full (patch, test) pair exceeds the model's context window. Despite the drop, 82% F1 at repo-level is strong enough to demonstrate the classification formulation transfers beyond function-level benchmarks. The 8B model's improvement to 84.8% shows scaling helps more at repo-level (3-point gain vs 2.5-point at function-level), consistent with longer contexts benefiting from more capacity. Per-class F1 ≥80% satisfies the best-tier threshold for all configurations.

name: LLM-as-Judge Baselines
description: Zero-shot Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B as LLM judges for both trajectory-level and per-test verification. Provides reference points for the accuracy-cost Pareto frontier.

tables.name: Table 17: Pareto Frontier — Accuracy vs Cost

analysis:
The LLM-judge baselines serve two roles: (1) they show fine-tuning is necessary, ruling out the "just prompt a big model" alternative; (2) they populate the Pareto frontier to demonstrate fine-tuned classification is cost-optimal. For EMNLP reviewers, this also connects to the broader NLP question of when task-specific fine-tuning beats general-purpose prompting — our answer is "for structured prediction tasks like execution simulation, fine-tuning a small model decisively beats prompting a large one."


Zero-shot LLM judges perform substantially below fine-tuned classifiers because execution simulation is not well-represented in pretraining data — models can reason about code semantics but haven't learned to reliably predict pass/fail outcomes without training signal. Qwen3-8B zero-shot achieves 67.1% trajectory F1, below even the CWM generation model (72.1%), because it lacks the fine-tuning that teaches output format and calibration. Qwen3-32B improves to 72.8% F1, roughly matching CWM at 4B — showing that 8× more parameters in zero-shot mode barely matches 4B fine-tuned generation. Per-test zero-shot is worse than trajectory-level zero-shot because models struggle to reason about individual test semantics without training. These baselines establish that fine-tuning is essential (not just prompting) and that the fine-tuned 4B classifier dominates the Pareto frontier (highest accuracy at lowest cost).

name: Per-test Majority Voting (K=3)
description: Run classification model 3 times per test with temperature sampling, take majority vote. Tests if self-consistency improves per-test accuracy at 3× inference cost.
analysis:
Appendix-level result. Shows self-consistency helps marginally but model scaling is a more efficient path to higher accuracy. The disagreement rate is potentially useful as a confidence calibration signal in deployment but is not explored further in this paper.

Majority voting at K=3 provides a modest 1.5-point F1 improvement (87.5 → 89.0) at 3× inference cost. The improvement is small because the base classifier is already well-calibrated at 87.5% — there's limited room for self-consistency to correct errors. The 13.4% disagreement rate (cases where not all 3 runs agree) identifies the model's uncertain predictions, which could be useful for selective abstention. However, the cost-accuracy tradeoff (1.5 pp for 3× cost) is unfavorable compared to simply using an 8B model (2.5 pp for ~2× cost). This experiment is included as a P2 result for completeness but is not central to any claim.
